utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two preliminary matters. The amended tape transcript is available for distribution. I'll perhaps distribute it to the Chamber now or at the break. I spoke yesterday of a note I had prepared on authorities -- not on authorities, on procedures in Germany, Austria, United Kingdom, Japan, and Australia. I didn't, in the event, distribute it. I certainly don't desire to go through it, but it is available, if the Chamber would find it helpful to have. It's about seven sides, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to hand it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In asking him to deal with it, I make it clear that the application is one which reflects the common sense and doesn't reflect, perhaps, the sometimes arbitrary and artificial rules of exclusion that the common law pursues, and it's an application that has the complete backing, of course, of the entire team. I'm reminded that perhaps I've erred in mentioning names in public. Not withstanding the disinclination of witnesses to come to the Tribunal, I suppose it's preferable not to use their names, if it's avoidable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, we saw yesterday that a chamber of a tribunal like ours cannot be deprived of evidence because a witness does not wish to come. We have seen the hypothesis of a witness who cannot come for a good reason, because he has died. Today we are dealing with another case of a witness who cannot appear because he will not appear. The hypothesis that we're addressing today raises two problems. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [redacted] Our Rules envisage various possibilities that a witness can be found in contempt of court. The text does not specify how such an unwilling witness can be forced to appear before this Tribunal, but in our view, it is quite possible to do so. Be that as it may, in this case, and in this stage of the proceedings, in view of the rather long delays by the Australian authorities, after you issued this order on the 22nd of November -- there was a notification on the 24th of January -- it does not appear opportune or desirable that measures of coercion be taken against this witness, and it is damaging for the image of the Tribunal, but that is a reality that we have to face up to at this stage of our proceedings. Beyond this question of the image, authority, and effectiveness of the orders issued by the Trial Chamber, the witness having given a negative answer and showing thereby what importance he attaches to those orders, and by this negative attitude, there is at least a technical, if not a legal impossibility of us making him come, we must nevertheless draw consequences regarding the administration of the evidence that this witness should have brought before you. We treat this witness as other persons having a common origin. Both having been members of the Vitez Brigade, we wanted these two witnesses to appear so that your Chamber could take into consideration the evidence that they have provided during the investigation. The specific situation, which has already been described by Mr. Nice, relating to these witnesses, we do not have the reports of their interviews collected by the investigators of the Tribunal. We have reports of interviews made by the authorities in Bosnia, the reports, the official reports, according to the accepted terminology in the region, taken in July 1993, in the course of which these two individuals, after having been interviewed by the military security of the Bosnian army, provided information and explained what their role had been within the Vitez Brigade before their arrest. We do not have any reports of investigators of the Tribunals, but we do have those official reports drawn up by the military security officers of Bosnia. As regards the first witness, the one who was notified of an order to appear in Australia, this one not only provided those statements to the military authorities, but was also interrogated by the investigators of that same service. And that interrogation was filmed at the time. In the course of that interrogation in the prison in which he was detained, the person explains the circumstances under which he was arrested, which unit he belonged to, that is the Vitez Brigade, who was his battalion commander, Karlo Grabovac, a name that you've already heard mentioned, and then he gave explanations for the reasons why he -- a human ear was found on him when he was captured. The video film shows by zoom this human organ on a table, quite a horrifying scene. The individual explained, and this also appears in the videotape and the official report drawn up at the time, that before going to the front with his comrade, he was promised, like other members of his unit, compensation if he brought trophies of a particular nature, in this case a human organ, an ear, or a finger. Obviously, the compensation would be higher if they were able to show that it was taken from a living person or from a corpse. And all this is indicated in the report. The information given by these two witnesses is information which we consider must be taken into consideration by your Chamber. This is information that has already been at least partially revealed to your Chamber during the testimony of the ECMM monitor, Mr. Morsink, who produced a report drawn up at the time by the ECMM, where reference was made to this compensation paid for human organs, or parts of human bodies by HVO soldiers. Therefore, you have already partially been informed of this by another source, and we hope that the witnesses will come and confirm this here in The Hague. And that is why we put both of them on our list of witnesses. Of course, these are special witnesses, because these two witnesses belonged to a unit under the command of the accused, Mario Cerkez, and it is not surprising, in view of the statements made at the time, that later on they changed their mind and refused to respond to your orders. And this was officially conveyed to us in January last year for the first witness, and the other witness, who still is in Vitez, has made it quite clear that he has no intention to appear before our Tribunal. Is that sufficient reason for you to go without this evidence relating to these facts, and to the participation of these individuals in acts committed in the Vitez area, especially with reference to the promise of compensation made by the accused, Mario Cerkez, in June, 1993? Because it was in June, 1993 that these two individuals were arrested by the Bosnian army services in Puticevo, that is a locality near Novi Travnik. We have compiled these elements of information. There is a videotape dated '93 of this witness who is in Australia. This witness was again contacted by our services in April, 1997, in Australia, where he was already a resident. And on that occasion there was another long video interview, in the presence of the Australian authorities. And in the course of that interview, the witness confirmed that he belonged to this brigade. He confirmed that his brigade commander was Mario Cerkez. But as regards the -- what he said about the taking of organs and the ear found in his possession, he denied that initial version, explaining that he was under pressure and under threat of violence that would be committed against him by those who were interrogating him. The report, and this video cassette that we have in our possession, is also at the disposal of your Chamber. Also, there are the statements that we recorded recently, from the time when we realised that it was highly improbable that these two witnesses would appear in The Hague, we considered it opportune to go and identify and interview people who might have met or heard them at the time, in June or July, 1993, when the official reports that I referred to a moment ago were drawn up. We were able to contact two of those people. One was an investigator of the security service in Zenica. The other was the warden of the prison in Zenica, where these two persons were detained. And these two people provided statements in which they explained how these two witnesses were questioned, and denied that any violence was committed against those two persons. Those two persons, if necessary, can be called to appear before the Tribunal to describe, once again, the circumstances under which those two witnesses were questioned in 1993, and the circumstances under which the ear was found on one of the two witnesses. We have prepared, for the benefit of the Chamber, a small dossier containing all the elements which we consider to be relevant to evaluate the importance of this evidence, the official reports I have mentioned. The videotapes of 1993 and 1997, the videos are quite readily available. And when one sees the first video, there is nothing especially suspicious regarding the statements made by the first witness. Also, there are no traces of any abuse during the interrogation. So it might be useful for your Chamber to see these two videos. The two reports of interviews taken by investigators in January last year have also been attached, as well as certain documents which show that these two witnesses were members of the brigade, of which the accused, Mario Cerkez, was the commander. We find ourself in a rather specific situation, because we do not have the records as we had in the cases we were discussing yesterday. But the records are not the only evidence that the Chamber should take into account. Rule 89 envisages a variety of evidence. And of course it does envisage the possibility of the Defence making its views known and its criticism known. It is up to your Chamber to make a decision and to review all this evidence, which we consider to be relevant under Rule 89. Mr. Nice has already said that the admission of this evidence is no particular problem in the civil law system. Where there is a freedom in the administration of evidence, the Chamber admits the documents, admits the depositions and testimonies, all the evidence are subject to its consideration, and are then weighed by the Chamber as regards its probative value and the weight to be attached to them. The evidence, as I have quickly reviewed it, have been compiled to form a small file for your kind attention, and we would like to ask you to be kind enough to receive that file. The system that I am familiar with, such a document would be prepared by the Prosecutor containing all the information, would be submitted to the Trial Chamber. When the Trial Chamber takes into consideration that -- and is convinced that everything has been done to bring the witness here, as is the case now, the Trial Chamber would take into consideration all that evidence, counting on the good faith of the Prosecutor that they had done everything possible to have the witness appear, noting that the witness being an unwilling witness. The Chamber would nonetheless take into consideration all the evidence relating to that witness and draw the necessary legal conclusions from it. I have tried to provide some clarification. And I would like to ask you, once again, to admit as evidence the information relating to the two witnesses that we had planned to call and which we regret to say will not be able to appear before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the case of the next four, are there any submissions to be made in relation to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there are any submissions, although there is a certain amount of up-to-date information that I can provide. Number five, I believe to be still unwilling. Number six, I think is now willing via video-link. And so I will be making a video-link application in due course, probably at the end of this procedural part of the case. Number seven is apparently now willing to come. And both these witnesses reveal the force of the Tribunal's orders. And I am happy to see that they are being responded to. Number eight is a witness in respect of whom the Chamber has a report on his ill health. He's a combination of unwilling and sick. It may be that he would be a potential candidate for a video-link, but not in the same place as number six, because number six would be in Bosnia, and number eight would be in Croatia. The only ruling I think I would want at the moment, pending discovering whether he is now willing, in light of the subpoena to give evidence via video-link -- any ruling I want at the moment is whether the Chamber is satisfied on the report on his ill health that he is indeed unable to travel to The Hague. That's one of his defences to giving evidence. Because if not, I will have to go and get further medical evidence. And in relation to paragraph C or Section C generally, our argument is that where every step is taken to bring a witness to Court and, through no fault of the Prosecution, the witness is not available to Court, even by reason of his or her own inclination, then it is still appropriate to read the witness's statement as the best available material that that witness could provide. The Chamber should know that even in relation to, for example, number five, we will attempt to get an affidavit from that witness, or formal statement. And I am going to ensure that that's done today or tomorrow, if I can. Notwithstanding her latest indication of disinclination to come here. There is, of course, a slight oddity about getting an affidavit from a witness who denies the authority of the Court's subpoena. But nevertheless, if an affidavit or formal statement can be taken, then that's better than not. The whole issue of contempt is for the Court's own initiative, I think, and not particularly from ours, we're not concerned about that, at least not at this stage. Where the witness is unwilling, as number 5 is, this witness has put the witness's judgement of risk above the judgement of either the OTP or the Court. Alternatively, the witness is simply being difficult for reasons known to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to interrupt you so that I can understand the position. We've got applications in respect of 3 and 4, on which we're going to rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, are you asking for any orders in respect of 5, 6, 7, and 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Well, in respect of -- no, because I've got outstanding action in respect of 5. Nothing there. In respect of 8, my only application at the moment is to know whether the Court is satisfied on the report that ill-health is established. Contingent on that, I will take my next steps in relation to that witness. And, of course, if a videolink is not possible, then I shall apply to have that witness's statement read, whether or not endorsed by an affidavit, on the grounds that he is sick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's for us to say whether he's too sick to come or not. I mean, we can deal with that in the context of an application to read his statement. It might be one of the matters we'd have to consider. But perhaps the simplest thing is to consider the position and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The report on his health was provided by the security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and, I think, as it were, directed to you. If the Court was not satisfied of his ill-health, then it might, I suppose -- no, I don't think it would issue a further subpoena, it's already issued this subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then Category D requires no action because the various subpoenas are being issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will consider the position. They are applied for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't mean to jump the gun there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider those, and it may be necessary to have a hearing. The matter which I have in mind is that the matter of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- which we are now up against.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we will consider those today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Category E.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Category E, the information of their ill-health is only recent. I am putting in hand today steps to provide evidence of their ill-health, and I will make an appropriate application in due course. The application, if the evidence of ill-health is sufficient, will be the simple one, that where witnesses are unable to attend court through good reason of ill-health, most systems, if not all, have a regime for permitting the adduction of some forms of statement, and we would say that the principles applying here would justify the reading of those statements. Of course, in relation to each of them, I will attempt to obtain affidavit-type statements, if possible. And I can add parenthetically that the good news is that despite the months or years of difficulties that we've had, now that the court in Bosnia is involved, it appears to be both working efficiently and, this is only informally communicated, happy to be involved. So that's good news. Category F --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just dealing with Category E, we will, I hope, be able to deal with those these week, as opposed to leaving the matter to later, so that we can rule on all these matters as expeditiously as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Category F, the position is that they are also unwilling, but they are put in a different category to the earlier unwilling witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But nonetheless, roughly the same principles may apply. So it may be convenient to deal with those together with the earlier category, Category B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, so far as 15 is concerned, I've distributed just this morning the short ex parte document containing information that I'd like the Chamber to consider in relation to him. Even apart from what is contained in the ex parte notice, or information, the very nature of the evidence he's capable of giving makes it unsurprising that he might be unwilling. On his account, not only did he see one of his companions murdered, but he was with the third member of the group, taken away by associates of the man he said was the murderer, beaten, and left effectively for dead. He lives in an area where there is still considerable presence of associates of the man he says was the murderer, and it is not at all surprising that he has the fears expressed. The Chamber will know that his position has been somewhat variable, and that not withstanding our acceptance that his fears are quite possibly well-founded, we continue to approach him in order both to see if he could be satisfied with measures of protection for which we could ask and, indeed, to see if he's going to be prepared to provide an affidavit; although, if his fears are justified, then an affidavit might be no better than giving evidence. But subject to any change of mind by him, subject to the provision of an affidavit, we would say that this matches many of the provisions currently operating in other countries where witnesses who are kept away by fear can have former statements read. Now, the statement of this witness, of course, is direct evidence of a killing by one of the defendants. The Chamber will want to remind itself of the way this evidence has been touched on so far. First, there was evidence from the very first witness in the case, initially to the effect that the crime scene was a suspicious crime scene and he didn't believe it to be a genuine crime scene, going to suggest that the killer was not the man named as the killer but someone else. In cross-examination, it emerged that there were accounts coming to him of who the true killer was. Further evidence to the same effect came from Dr. Mujezinovic and from another witness, a woman with whom with witness, witness number 15, was originally expected to attend at court. He failed to attend right at the last minute. That female witness gave an account, as the Chamber may recall, of what witness 15 had said to her, and it would, in our respectful submission, be surprising, and perhaps almost illogical, not to at least take the best version of witness 15's account that will be available to the Chamber, and depending on his attitude, the best account will either be his witness statement as it presently is or possibly his witness statement confirmed by a statement made at the local court. The Chamber will remember that the evidence of this killing, which is not specifically charged, goes to the attitude and response of the defendant concerned to the law at the time, and is by way of general but important background. So adduction of this evidence in one form or another doesn't offend any of the particular rules of exclusion in the European law which we were referred very generally yesterday. Our submission is that the absence of the witness, if he remains unwilling to attend, is understandable and justified and that it is entirely appropriate to take the best version of his evidence, as that may turn out to be in due course. As to 16, the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you leave 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- you referred to a document handed in in relation to him. I've got the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We filed it this morning. It may be on your legal officer's desk. The usher knows where it is because we gave it to him this morning. It's only one side. The Chamber will remember that I was concerned about the additional information coming to me, and that I made it clear that although I would serve material ex parte, I would, of course, understand whatever decision the Chamber made about making that further information more generally available; although if it is to be made more generally available, most certainly in a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's somewhere in the Registry. Let's have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have further copies done, and we'll make those copies available to you informally, as soon as may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll need the copies before we can consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. So far as witness 16 is concerned, he's a witness whose evidence has been available to the Chamber, and, as we know, would be able to give very wide evidence on the conflict generally. But he gives evidence of a particular meeting with the first defendant, and it's only on that topic that we wanted his evidence. He gives the fullest account of the circumstances in which Mr. Kordic was to be found at the Tisovac headquarters; of his wearing uniform, including, as this witness says, insignia; and he gives an account of Mr. Kordic's reaction to the interview that the witness wanted to have with him; and he gives an account of something that Mr. Kordic thereafter said about not wanting to share somebody else's fate. It's plainly potentially helpful evidence. It's plainly understandable why the witness may not be willing to attend. I am aware that there are other reasons why he's not willing to attend as well, all linked to the ethnic divisions, I think, at the time and continuing. And the Chamber has formed the view that his failure to respond to the subpoena is not unjustified. Again, this is not evidence that is evidence on which alone any conviction of anything could be returned; it's a piece of evidence, in the large jigsaw of evidence that cases like this involve, its adduction would not offend the law of this institution or the law of the European Convention, and we would say again, as with number 15, that it would be right for the Chamber to have the best version of that witness's evidence that may be available, which, at this stage, is his statement. It may be, I don't know, it may be that we can obtain from the place where he presently lives an affidavit, or something in the form of an affidavit. But again, he may take the view, as may witness 15, that an affidavit is no better in terms of risk than giving evidence in person. So those are the applications I make for F. In relation to Category G, by way of information, I can simply tell the Court that number 17 and 20 have already been dealt with by the local court; number 18 lives in another country, and it may not be possible to get an affidavit between now and the close of the case, but if it is, I will provide one; numbers 21, 22, and 23 are being dealt with today by the Court, as I understand it; number 24 is also still in the process of being dealt with, and I hope soon to be dealt with conclusively. I think that's all I have to say about those witnesses. The document in relation to witness 15 is being photocopied. Yes. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful to have 16's statement. We have got a copy of that. I have no doubt we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I think mine, in fact, is unmarked. And I can rip that out and make it available straightaway. It's not unmarked, but it's only got odd highlights on it. And I'll mark the page. It's a long statement. I'll hand it in and I'll mark the page where he deals with meeting the first defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. So the matters we'll rule on now are three and four and 15 and 16. And we are asked to make a ruling in relation to number eight, about whether he is too sick to travel or not. But that's something we'll have to consider. But we'll hear submissions that the Defence want to make on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just say generally, Mr. President, starting out, that the first time we saw this list, of course, was yesterday afternoon. The Court's well aware, I'm sure, of the reading obligations that have been imposed on us over the last two weeks. This is another 24 witness statements, and series of statements that we would have to consume. And I have to confess, we simply have not had the time; preparing, as we were, for cross-examination of two witnesses today and other matters. With respect to witnesses three and four, I have absolutely no idea what the Prosecution is talking about or the flow of dialogue that's apparently been occurring between the Court and the Prosecution regarding these witnesses, as well as 15 and 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no mystery about this. This is where applications have been made for subpoenas, and the response is what you've heard, that these witnesses are unwilling to come. So you can take it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the witnesses being unwilling to come, if they are unwilling to come, they are unwilling to come. They shouldn't be permitted to testify. It's simply an open invitation to trample into the ground the defendant's fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Tribunal Statute, and to eliminate, at the request of the Prosecution, the right to cross-examine enshrined in Rule 85. And, as a matter of principle, that's our position. I can certainly see in some situations of exceptional circumstances, such as the death of a witness, where the witness statement bears on peripheral rather than central matters, an exception being made under those circumstances. But coming from where I come from, the notion of the Prosecution in a criminal case offering an unsworn statement that's never been tested by cross-examination, would never be admitted in any court in which I practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no exception to the hearsay rule, in favour of a witness kept away by fear or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In terms of the State practice, Your Honour, in Virginia, absolutely not. In terms of the Federal practice, there are, as the Court's well aware, a series of Federal rules of civil and criminal procedure. In the civil side, the hearsay exceptions are found in Rules 803, where there are, I think, 24 separate exceptions to the hearsay rule. The ones that we are talking about are not -- are not part of those rules. And then Rule 804, which deals with situations of unavailability and death. But I do not believe that simply because, for example, Mr. -- witness number 3, for example. I mean, I really do not have any idea what the situation is with respect to this witness, but apparently he was at one point willing, another point unwilling. We would simply suggest to the Court that if he can't be bothered to come to the Court, then his witness statement shouldn't be considered in evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Supposing he says, for the moment, that he is in fear of coming. And supposing a totally different fact, but in a national jurisdiction, a criminal keeps a witness away. I mean, not an uncommon practice these days, certainly in some countries, is to intimidate its witnesses. Now, as a matter of principle, what should a Court do about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of principle, Your Honour, these two gentlemen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am not talking about these two gentlemen. I am talking hypothetically, Mr. Sayers. Supposing criminals, not necessarily the accused in a case, but supposing criminals frighten witnesses, so they say, "I am too frightened to come." What then should a Court do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, Mr. President, we would respectfully submit that what the Court should and must do is to provide some means where the defendant's confrontation rights are respected. After all, obviously the Prosecution should be free to go around collecting bits and pieces of apparently peripheral evidence, and central evidence in some respects, certainly. With respect to witness number 3, I guess the evidence could be said to be somewhat important to one of the defendants. But it's -- the defendants do have confrontation rights, and those are central rights. In fact, they are arguably some of the only rights that criminal defendants have in a tribunal like the International Tribunal. The confrontation rights, we think, have been pretty effectively exercised here. And there is another point that I would like to make with respect to the use of witness statements untested by cross-examination. And that's the situation that we have seen with Dr. Mujezinovic and others. Dr. Mujezinovic, for example, specifically pointed out errors in a witness statement to an investigator. And those errors were never corrected. And that's a real problem. But under cross-examination, he pointed out those errors and so the Court was apprised of his various versions of what the truth would be. I don't know why the Prosecution is bending over backwards to attempt to deprive the defendants in this case of their confrontation rights. What's wrong with a deposition under Rule 71? Certainly the Rules provide for it. It could be done under a pseudonym, in a foreign country, and then the deposition could be admitted under seal in this case. There would be no way that the evidence would get out to the world at large, or no way in which the particular declarant, I think, would be justified in any fears for his testimony. If everything --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Sayers. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- so-to-speak. Even though that course is obviously fraught with its own problems, in light of the obligation of the Tribunal to ensure a fair and public trial for each of the defendants. So that's the matter in principle. These people are available to be cross-examined. They are available to be confronted. Why not adopt a procedure, if they are genuinely unwilling, and the Court is genuinely satisfied that their concerns are real and justified, why not impose a regime where the defendants do have confrontation rights, rather than straining and stretching for in some way which deprives the defendant of those confrontation rights? And those are, as I said before, and I am not going to repeat myself, but those are precious rights. We hold them as precious. And as a matter of principle, they shouldn't be discarded blithely in 24 separate instances, in addition, I might point out, to the 25 or so transcript witnesses, whose transcripts have already been admitted without particular rights of confrontation for either one -- either defendant. I don't have a total count -- I think it's 95 witnesses who have testified so far. As far as we can gather, it looks like there are going to be something like 110 witnesses who testify live in this case. If you add to that, 25 witnesses who have not testified live, and 24 witnesses whose statements or what have you will be admitted in some other fashion, that's fully 50 per cent, or nearly 50 per cent of the witnesses who will have given evidence in this case, will not have been exposed to cross-examination. The defendant will never have the right to see them, let alone confront them and test the veracity of their story. And that's a really significant issue. I would respectfully represent to the Trial Chamber, it's one which genuinely concerns us. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not your concerns which we want to hear. It's your submissions. I meant to tell Mr. Lopez-Terres the same thing, when he said we had to -- the Trial Chamber must consider something or other. It's not for counsel to put it that way. With respect, it's your submissions we want. Anyway, your submission is that this is a matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with respect to the first witness -- the third witness, rather, we understand that he has actually recanted the first statement, which the Prosecution wants to have admitted into evidence. Surely, under no system of justice, would a recanted statement, untested by cross-examination, be admitted into evidence. That's our submission, and I'm sure that Mr. Kovacic will have more to say on that. With respect to the only other witness that apparently concerns us, witness 16, we are uninformed. We simply have no information regarding the circumstances under which this witness does not want to testify, or would be excused from testifying. But, clearly, he is available to be deposed under Rule 71, if that's deemed to be appropriate. And if he doesn't want to come to Court, or can't be bothered to come to Court, whatever the situation is, then clearly, in order to protect the confrontation rights that are enshrined in the Rules and in the Statute, then we should be permitted to have some opportunity to confront and cross-examine him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] If I may, I should like first to pronounce myself on the Category B. That is witnesses three and four. But, to make it quite clear, we naturally object to these witnesses, and I shall explain why. Even though I do not think it is particularly legally relevant, but I think the Prosecution went into recounting the case. And I must also touch upon that. And then also address the legal elements, which I believe the Court must have in mind, and which are against the admission of such statements. As for the facts mentioned by the Prosecution, I do not think it transpired quite clearly, from what they said, that witness 3 and witness 4 had been detained in the military police prison of the BH army for a whole year. They were among the last to be released by the BH army at the time when the Washington Accords were signed. And there, they made statements, according to them, not under duress, but under torture, and this was confirmed by witness 3, who then stated before the Australian authorities and said why and how he told the military police of the BH army all that they wanted to hear. Under the law which was in force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the event, which is the Criminal Proceedings Act, both statements which those witnesses gave to the investigation authorities are completely wrongful. Firstly, they were interrogated as prisoners of war; that is, running counter to international conventions, because prisoners of war could not be interrogated on the subjects they were interrogated; secondly, or alternatively, if they were not prisoners of war, if they were simply civilian, it means then, under the then Criminal Proceedings Act, that witness 3 could not have been interviewed because he was underage, and under no conditions, with no exceptions, could his statement be used in a possible criminal case. So I'm talking about a criminal case which could have been started against that witness, or either the accused in that hypothetical case, before the Bosnian authorities, pursuant to the then legislation, or today's legislation. As he was a minor, he would have had to be interviewed by a special judge for minors. In the law, and I'm not going now to quote various articles, and so forth -- but we do, of course, bring those quotes, those articles from the law -- but their law envisages absolutely no exceptions under which such a statement could be used in criminal proceedings. And, as I said, in Australia, he explained what was the weight, how trustworthy was that statement. Now, the question arises as to what does the term "unwilling witness" mean, or "hostile." Not even hypothetically. Can we talk here about decisions of a witness based on the ethnic division which we have in this case? The two witnesses, 3 and 4, are Croats by ethnicity, and witness 3 is in Australia, he lives in Australia, which is a democratic country; a country where various instruments of power, no doubt, work; in a country where a court can issue an order to bring such a witness under custody. So the question of whether one is willing or unwilling does not arise in this particular case. I'm not going to infer from that that the Prosecution does not really want this witness to come, because he's happier with papers which cannot be subject to cross-examination. But whatever the legal system we are talking about, first, a witness is called. If the witness refuses, then every system provides for some other instrument which courts have at their disposal, for instance, if one issues an order, a subpoena, and then you have also some enforcement authority. Let us look at Bosnia, and I'm referring to witness 4. The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina unquestionably cooperates with this Tribunal; there are countless examples of this, and there is no need to talk about this. There are authorities there who work and who are willing to comply with the orders of the Tribunal, and moreover, there are also international forces who brought even the accused, not only witnesses, to this Tribunal. So we cannot draw a sign of equality -- and this is the initial thesis of the Prosecution -- we cannot draw a sign of equality between dead and unwilling witnesses, unless the witness himself or herself comes to the court and says, "I don't want to testify," and there again, there are instruments which can be used to make them do so. Meanwhile, although you must give us some reasonable time, but yesterday after the session, we requested medical documentation for the witness who is in Bosnia, that is, witness 4. So far, I have obtained only some indirect information that this person is unaccountable and has been unaccountable since he was released from Zenica. I have asked my assistants to get this documentation. I believe that some documents have been found, and we shall get it tonight, at least something will be faxed to us. Of course, I do not know whether that is true or not. But I have information about both, that they have suffered significant psychological, mental damage after their stay in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you offered this explanation, but could you say how the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in Croatia, would view the admission of a statement of a witness who was unwilling to come to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Criminal Proceedings Act, which was in effect at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croatia --- and as you already know, both these republics took over the laws of the former Federation, and recently a new Criminal Proceedings Act was adopted in Croatia. I have not had time to study it, but my colleague, perhaps, can. But under the then laws, there was absolutely no exception under which a statement made to the police could be used as evidence in a criminal case, there was not a single exception to that rule. The only exception was when a statement had been made before an investigating magistrate, an investigating judge. So it is a statement made under oath, under a threat, in case of false testimony, because that was also a criminal offence; that is, the investigator had to caution the witness that false testimony is a criminal offence under this or that article of the law, and punishable by 3 to 5 years of penal solitude. And after that, the judge takes the statement, and there is a clause in the law which says that a witness can, of course, change the record, object to various parts of it, so on and so forth -- let me not go into that -- and subsequently, when the hearing begins, that is, when it comes before the trial chamber, this witness must again appear before the court, as a rule. Now, in that particular case, there is an exception, when this statement given to the investigating judge may be read. The provisions are very restrictive in this regard, and my colleague, who is really an expert on the procedural law, if a witness has died in the meantime or -- but he is not even sure. That is very restrictive. But I'm referring only to a statement made before an investigating judge. As for a statement which this same witness, or any other witness, or the accused, made before the police or, rather, the investigating authorities, before the case has reached the judge, this statement not only may not be read, but this same judge, that is, the investigating judge, was bound to single out that file, seal it, and keep it separately from the rest of the file; that is, it could not be read. These statements made to the police could be used only by the investigating judge by way of preparation for the first statement, for the first interrogation of the accused, for the first interview of the accused, for the first questioning of the accused, by the investigating authorities. And after that, the investigating judge had to seal it, put it away, and nobody else could see it. So under the domestic legislation, and we can bring it, of course, under the domestic legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because this is what is relevant here, there was no other mechanism according to which a statement of an unwilling witness could be read in the course of the main hearing. The category, as defined here, "Unwilling Witnesses," did not exist in the law, because the law had a mechanism whereby measures could be used to ensure the presence of a witness before the court. So first was the summons, and the second was a subpoena or, rather, bringing a witness under custody. If a witness would refuse, then the court would order the police to bring in the witness for a particular hearing. Now, also with regard to witnesses 3 and 4, just for your information, if the whole story were built on such indirect positions -- as are those of the Prosecutor, I must say, even though it might not be legally relevant; but it has to do with facts we're dealing with -- and that is, in Bosnia, especially in Central Bosnia, in 1993, and I did examine witnesses about this, not a single body without an ear had been found. So, my question is: Whence the ear, if there is no corpse? But we continue working on it and perhaps we shall find something. Another relevant point to my mind is -- I believe we saw here, and Mr. Sayers already mentioned it, but we heard a series of witnesses, not one or two, but quite a large number, and I am not quoting figures at random, of who did not say anything that has not been found in the statements given to investigators or the Bosnian police services during the war. Not only that, quite a number of witnesses have said things which contradicted the statements given earlier to investigators. And those statements have proven highly unreliable and not safe ground for any conclusions. This relates particularly to the statements given to the commission for war crimes in Bosnia or different military authorities or police authorities. As for witness 15, which, in Prosecutor's words, has reason not to be willing to come or, rather, justifiably unwilling, and this is again a category which I really cannot endorse. Our learned friends from the Prosecution quoted other corroborative statements, but they omitted to mention certain things, needless to say. Such as, for instance, that one of the statements made here before the Court and the document which was adduced with that witness, and he was an intelligence officer of the Bosnian army in which he said that war criminals from the area, and he mentioned war criminals from the area of Vitez. In the document he is accused of the murder in question. The person who was also mentioned, also a witness. That is the case 30 May '92. That was in the hotel, in Vitez Hotel. And that is why that exhibit was adduced, that is, the investigation on site, immediately after the crime. Now, in that record, and I really don't remember, five or seven policemen, by the civilian, military policemen, HVO and BiH army, that is both parties, because we are talking about May '92. And nobody ever, except for the witness whom we heard here, that is one of the policemen, expressed ever any doubts regarding that particular incident. So rumours started sometimes, and then the witness said here, and then after the investigation rumours started that somebody else must have killed that victim. And this is, I believe, what the statement of number 15 is all about. In other words, we have quite a lot of evidence about it. The Defence will already produce some evidence -- if witness [redacted] would come, we would be very happy to see him here, because we should indeed like to cross-examine him. And if he cannot come, then his statement may not be read. I think that the witness is accessible and available, because, after all, there are tools and means which can be used to bring him. If the Court wishes to hear some more detailed -- I really do not want to quote all of the articles, but if you wish to receive any more detailed information about the Criminal Proceedings Act in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Croatia, in '92, '93, I know that Mr. Naumovski is quite ready to explain the legislation in greater detail. Or give us a bit more time -- a little more time and we shall prepare it in a day or two. We object to this primarily because we are losing the right to cross-examine and important matters are at stake. And therefore we object against the introduction of the statements they made to the investigating authorities or different other authorities. And we are absolutely not willing, not ready to waive our rights to cross-examine them. Perhaps I was not sufficiently methodical, sufficiently systematic in presenting our case in this particular case, but we were not quite ready for it. We really expected to see two witnesses, so there was a lot of documents to study, and we are getting ready for those two witnesses, but did not expect this discussion. Witness 5, I am afraid, I mentioned his name. This, I hope, will be struck out from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make a couple of points on behalf of both myself and Mr. Lopez-Terres. Nearly all these witnesses were listed as witnesses for whom we wanted affidavits and so on in our updated overview. Confrontation rights are to be contrasted, as Mr. Lopez-Terres explained yesterday, with other methods for attacking the credibility of a witness, or the believability of a witness. There is no question of our bending over backwards to put in written statements. We are taking whatever steps we can to get the material before the court in a proper and most timely way. Depositions simply aren't available for one reason or another, so far as the witnesses in Category B or Category F are concerned. It's not a possibility. If somebody is not cooperating at all, as in Category B, or frightened, as in Category F, then depositions simply aren't a possibility. The general point on the law of other countries that's being made has to be contrasted with the fact and reality that this institution doesn't have investigating judges. That's not the system it introduced. The Chamber will note that all written statements are topped and tailed, begun and ended with assertions as to the truth. Those statements go as far as it's possible within the rules to go, to become a statement by oath, which is of course why Judge Jorda took the view, in dealing with one of these statements that we dealt with yesterday, that it was indeed a statement on oath. Dealing with Mr. Kovacic's points about Australia's powers. The Chamber knows that in relation to all these witnesses, we have taken the process of coercion to the end of the line. And we can do no more. That indeed makes us rather parallel, the Chamber may think, with the example he gave for Bosnia, of police bringing in a person for questioning, in relation, for example, to Category B. That's exactly what we have attempted, but his attitude, and the Australian's response, and of course the decision of this Chamber, means that we haven't been able to do that. As to whether the person being under age is significant in wartime. The fact is that it's our rules that apply and, as Mr. Lopez-Terres reminds me, in relation to that particular witness, when the suggestion is that what he said may be unreliable, of course he wasn't just saying that he admitted things, which is perhaps what happens when forced by interrogators. He was actually giving a coherent account of responsibility lying elsewhere. And the Chamber reminds itself, perhaps, that the investigators taking those interviews are available to be called to explain the propriety of them, and indeed to explain the finding of the ear. Finally, so far as 15 and 16 are concerned, the Chamber will recognise that -- I hope, that we probably applied a stiffer test for the witnesses than we might have done, for only in respect of the one witness did we ourselves say, we think these expressed fears are so potentially realistic that we shouldn't attempt coercion. And once we made that judgement, that was the position we morally had to take. We couldn't say, "We think he is justified in the fears that he has," and then ask the Court to rule. Because the Court had indicated, in relation to number 16, that that wasn't the way it wanted it done. We made the decision, and there is only, in respect to the one witness at the end, that we've been taken to that position. And the Chamber may think that it's an entirely responsible and understandable position to take, particularly in light of its own ruling in relation to number 16. I can't help you further, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider these matters now. We'll sit again at half past 11.00, unless you hear to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement, you have one coming. I have simply put a tag beside the relevant passage. There are some more coming, so that I'll have them -- if the usher makes himself available, they can be brought to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me have that. Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will give the Trial Chamber's ruling in relation to the material which was sought to be admitted. The four witnesses whose statements the Prosecution seek to adduce are described as "unwilling witnesses." In one way or another, they have refused to come to give evidence. They are, therefore, in a different category from the witnesses with whom we dealt yesterday, who were dead. These witnesses are available but have refused, for one reason or another, to come. We make no general ruling about witnesses in such a category; it is not necessary to do so at this stage, save to say this, that it seems to us that such witness statements from such witnesses may be admissible under Rule 89(C). If, for instance, a witness is genuinely in fear and is kept away, intimidated, because of the actions of an accused or on behalf of an accused, a Trial Chamber may then admit such evidence. But it will depend on the circumstances of each case and it will depend on the probative nature of the evidence. I turn to deal with the four witnesses with whom we've been dealing this morning. Numbers 3 and 4 on the Prosecution's list, described as "unwilling/hostile," these two witnesses have simply refused to come, there's no good reason for their absence, and that in itself may be a ground for excluding their evidence. If a witness is simply not prepared to come, then the Trial Chamber should think long and hard about admitting that evidence. The circumstances of this case, they also need to be mentioned. These statements were made, and filmed in one case, while, at least in one case, the witness was in detention and being interrogated by the authorities of the opposite side. One of the witnesses has since retracted his statement, and it's now alleged that these statements were obtained under duress and, indeed, torture. Now, there may or may not be any truth in that, we're not going to rule, but that casts doubt, or must cast doubt upon the reliability of the statements, and in those circumstances, to admit the statement without any proper cross-examination may be to admit totally unreliable evidence. For those reasons, the circumstances of the refusal and the circumstances in which these statements were taken, the statements are not admitted, nor, of course, is any film attached to them. Numbers 15 and 16 are in a different category. They are described as "justified unwilling," which may not be a very elegant way of putting it, but probably sums up the position; namely, those who may have good reason not to give evidence. In fact, in relation to number 16, the Trial Chamber had indicated on another occasion that it accepted that this witness was in fear. In the case of number 15, we have seen material which, it is suggested, has put the witness in fear. We are not satisfied, in his case, that he is in fear. That would be sufficient to exclude his statement. But dealing with it, he gives direct evidence implicating one of the accused in a murder, and it is the view of the Trial Chamber that such evidence should not be admitted without cross-examination and, in particular, in this case. Given that the Trial Chamber is not satisfied as to the reasons for his not coming and are not satisfied as to the correctness of admitting such evidence without cross-examination, it will be excluded. Number 16 is in a different position, as I said. It was accepted that he was genuinely in fear. However, having looked at the evidence that he was to give, the Trial Chamber is of the view that it is cumulative, there's been much evidence on the topic on which the Prosecution sought to rely in his case, and it's therefore not sufficiently probative to admit it in these circumstances without cross-examination. Accordingly, the statements of all four will be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me now turn to the matters of the map. There are some further administrative matters that I'll deal with, but it's probably better if I deal with them at the end of the day, when I may have more information about the position on outstanding affidavits and matters of that sort, to bring the Chamber up to date. Mr. Lopez-Terres is going to deal with the map, or maps. There is a -- I'll go back. The maps were responsive to an inquiry of the Trial Chamber before the summer recess, and, indeed, the inquiry was, I think, both as to front-line positions and deployments. The witness has prepared a report which has been served on the Chamber, and I'm not sure if the Chamber has got it in enough copies for each member of the Chamber to read it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got a summary. Is the report this other binder that we now have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, the report is 13 pages. The very substantial binder you have is simply the supporting material, in case questions of detail are to be raised. And subject to one or two reservations, it's probably a document or an exhibit best produced as a single exhibit, supporting the witness's report. There is one reservation. We can come to that later. But if the Chamber's had an opportunity to, and has read the 13-page report of the witness, then it would be my submission that, through Mr. Lopez-Terres, the most efficient and swift method of dealing with the evidence would be to get the witness to give first his explanation of the three maps. There are two on the board already, and there is another one which is on the floor, which will have to take its place with some overlays in due course. And then, perhaps, to move summarily through the contents of the report. But I think that the maps are things that he can speak of himself, without going through the process of formal examination-in-chief. He can simply present the maps to you. And I think you'll find that quite helpful. It may be there are some technical objections by the Defence and, in one way or another, I think I'll hand over to Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have several objections relating to the actual report. In principle, however, I do not believe we have any objection to the witness testifying as to his understanding of the front lines and the actual troop dispositions. And that was the precise request upon which the Trial Chamber made of the Prosecution, which would be of assistance, given the plethora of maps which confessedly are rather confusing in this case. It would be useful to have in one place a statement of where the front lines were, at specific points in time, and where the brigades of the various opposing forces were. And, accordingly, I want to make it absolutely clear that we do not object to that in principle. It's the report that I would like to address to the Trial Chamber's attention. And one of the problems that we have with it, is that it's based partially upon inadmissible materials and other materials, such as, for example, footnote 1, was two maps from, apparently, the Armija, BiH. We only received these about 15 minutes ago, as a matter of fact. And a significant quantity of the conclusions, apparently, in the report are based upon this. I'll be frank with the Trial Chamber, that I've not had an opportunity to evaluate these in any detail. And the scale of them is such that apparently there are two tables on one of these maps. That's referred to in footnote 1. They are absolutely illegible, but apparently they supposedly contain an evaluation, at least from the ABiH side, of the relative strength of the opposing forces. That's one problem that we have. Another problem is that there was no request made for a 13-page written report. Frankly, this report tiptoes, on more than one occasion, into the area of expert testimony, and there has not been a compliance with Rule 94 bis. Putting that aside for a moment, the report is also based, if you take a look at footnotes 41 and 62 of the report, upon a witness statement of a witness who has not testified before this Tribunal, from Zepce, and whose statement was not included in the Zepce binder. Which is, we would respectfully represent, one more continuing effort to sneak witness statements into evidence in this case. Equally significant, and I address the Court's attention to footnotes 38, 58, 60, and 67, there are portions of General Blaskic's testimony that have been consulted and relied upon in coming up with the conclusions that are contained in this report. In addition, it doesn't stop there. If you take a look at footnote 49, on page 7 of the report, there is reliance placed upon testimony from other witnesses in the Blaskic case, who have testified in this case, but not on that point. Mr. McLeod being the case in point. Similarly, if you take a look at footnote 71, I believe I am correct in saying that there are exhibits that were introduced in the Blaskic case, such as, for example, a letter written to trial counsel in the Blaskic case, Mr. Nobilo, introduced as exhibit Defence 440(a) in that case, but not, I believe, introduced into evidence in this case. And there are many other materials that have not been supplied. And there are just a couple of other points that I would like to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention. This report actually goes significantly beyond a description of the front lines and an explanation of the deployments of the various units of the Central Bosnia operative zone, and the 3rd Corps, which is what was requested. There are analyses, for example, of the HVO intentions to establish front lines based upon three orders issued by General, or then Colonel Blaskic, on April the 17th, 1993. And it's not apparent from the report, and it's not apparent to me, why it was felt necessary to include that explanation or analysis of what the apparent intentions of the HVO were with respect to the matter of front lines on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I am going to stop you. It seems sensible to do this: To hear the witness as to the maps, which apparently he's going to address first, and then, if we want to hear any more, we'll consider it, and hear your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may contribute to this. I am sharing the opinion of my learned colleague, Mr. Sayers. I would just like to inform also -- to inform also the Chamber that there were discussions between, as we informed the Chamber earlier, you will remember, between the Prosecution desk and Defence, both Defences. We did exchange some written proposals and comments, and then we met. And some limited progress was done towards the idea to narrow the disputed issues. However, a lot of that remains open, which I would like also to stress, that there is one thing which also should be somehow at least clearly stated, and I guess also decided by the Chamber. It is the principal issue, whether this material produced in front of us, and I am referring to both maps and the report, should be based exclusively on the exhibits already tendered in this case, or is it -- or whether we can allow to have also the exhibits used which are not tendered in this case. I don't have any particular opinion, whether that would be allowed or not, but at least it should be clearly stated. So whatever will be produced today, it is not based only on the exhibits already tendered in this case. So we should be aware of that. And besides, there -- some of the details which my colleague mentioned, I would like to mention just one. And of course it would be raised during the cross, but just as an example of methodology which was used. One of -- most important parts of this presentation for my client is the positions of the brigades on 17 April. According to the Blaskic orders, there were three of them on that date. However, there is no particular presentation on the position of the brigade on the 16th, which is really the critical day, when conflict started. And, of course, that could be raised, but it was simply omitted. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I suggest that -- as I said before, that the witness gives his evidence about the maps and we'll see how we get on. And if it becomes necessary, we'll have to give some rulings. But at least at the moment he must be entitled to produce his maps, and then you can ask him how he came to those conclusions, if there are matters in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That would help. Your Honour, if I may, we don't know now whether the report will be admitted as separate evidence or only his presentation and the maps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to hear his evidence about the maps. We are then going to consider whether it's necessary to have the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Take a seat. Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are Mr. Jon Elford, and you are 29 years old?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. My full name, Jonathan Elford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are working as a military analyst with the Office of the Prosecutor in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been exercising these duties since October 1997.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: For the Tribunal, yes, for the last few years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in a few words, what the duties of a military analyst consist of?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The normal duties -- I was really given some form of direction, a task to carry out, which normally would be something in the line of producing reports on military-based subjects, analysing a military action or an organisation and chain of commands. The analyst would then, using all the available information, make an analysis of the information and produce or refine a report based on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You belong to a group of some 15 analysts working for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, since last summer, you were asked to work on maps, at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor, within the framework of the Kordic trial. This request was, in fact, in response to a question by the Chamber on the 3rd of August, 1999, when the Chamber requested that a map be presented on which certain information would appear regarding the deployment of forces in the region, the BiH forces, the HVO forces, and the army of Republika Srpska. You personally worked on those maps, you produced those maps. There is a map of Central Bosnia for April 1993, another map for the month of July, and finally, you also worked on a map for the Vitez region on which you made three transparencies to show us the situation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct. The deployment shown relates to the HVO and the ABiH, with a VRS front line shown as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within these maps, you will explain to us in detail in a few minutes the confrontation lines in different colours, as well as a listing of various combat units both for the BiH army and the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you if you would be kind enough to begin and explain the first map that you worked on, commenting on the various indications or signs appearing on that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we have an exhibit number, Mr. Lopez-Terres, for the first map?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map, dated April, as well as the map for July, is marked Z2612.2A and Z2612.2B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I'll, first of all, explain the map. This is a 1:100.000 scale map of Central Bosnia, which I believe has already been presented as an exhibit in the trial. So 1:100.000 scale means that one centimetre on the map is equivalent to one kilometre on the map. The map shows information on the terrain of the area, road systems, and towns or villages in the area, but it's also been overprinted with obstruction information, which relates to overhead obstacles such as pylons and electricity cables, which are actually not part of this presentation. I'll move on to the actual information shown. The first line which is on the map for April 1993 was the VRS front line, and this line is shown in red, following this area [indicates], the front line around the Sarajevo area [indicates], and then the northern area [indicates]. This front line was made up basically from UNPROFOR traces which were made at the time, and then also with comparison to ABiH maps which were made after the events. They were quite consistent, there was a fair amount of consistency between the two of them. Really, this front line remained relatively stable for the entire period we're looking at, and so it's been used again for the second map, for July onwards. The other information shown then is the HVO and ABiH actual brigade-sized units and the corps headquarters, and what is shown is the brigade headquarters and not the whole area that the brigade actually covered. So a brigade would be able to cover an area away from its headquarters. If I go through, first of all, the HVO brigades, the first one marked is number 1, and that is the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; below that, number 2, is the Viteska Brigade, which operated in the Vitez area; number 3, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, operating in Busovaca; and number 4, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, in Novi Travnik. Then in the Travnik area. Number 5, the Travnicka Brigade, and outside Travnik, the Frankopan Brigade; number 7 on the map is the Jure Francetic Brigade, which is the HVO brigade for the Zenica area; number 8, the 111th Brigade in the Zepce area. And then I move down to the Bobovac Brigade in Vares; the Kotromanic Brigade in Kakanj; the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak. Then in Bugojno, the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, and in Gornji Vakuf, the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade. In the same way, the ABiH brigades have also been plotted on the map. So if I go through those in order, all based in the Zenica area, were the headquarters of the 3rd Corps ABiH, the 301st Brigade, the 303rd, the 314th, and then the 7th Brigade ABiH. In the Travnik area, this part of the map [indicates], we had the 306th Brigade, the 312th, and also the 17th Brigade. If I move across the map to Novi Travnik [indicates] is the location of the 308th Brigade; and then following the map around, in Bugojno was the 307th Brigade; Gornji Vakuf, the 317th Brigade; move to the north of the map, in Zavidovici, the 318th Brigade; in Zepce, the 319th Brigade. Based just to the west of Kakanj, we have the 305th Brigade; in Kakanj itself, is number 13, the 309th Brigade; Kacuni, outside Busovaca, was the 333rd Brigade; in Visoko were the 302nd Brigade; and then in Breza was the 304th Brigade. Back to the brigade for the Vitez area, based in Poculica, is the 325th Brigade. And those are the brigade-sized units for the area which have been plotted on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not mark on this map certain units of a smaller size than brigades. They were units that were referred to in the course of this trial, so could you comment on them?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That is correct. Basically, to avoid cluttering the map, we kept it to brigade-sized units. But also for the HVO, there are other smaller-sized units, which I mentioned in the report, which were the Vitezovi special forces unit which operated within the Vitez pocket; the Tvrtko II special forces unit, which was based in Nova Bila, which again is in an area north of Vitez; the 4th Battalion of the military police, which was a military police unit for the HVO for the Central Bosnia area; and then it also mentions the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade and the Ante Bruno Busic Brigade, which operated in this area sometime in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two last units that you mentioned came from Herzegovina, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's right. They were deployed in Central Bosnia in approximately January 1993. We've seen this from orders of General Blaskic at the time to these units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You acted in the same way, a little later, for the year 1993, and then you drew a second map on which you indicated again the confrontation lines, and also the units that were deployed. The number of those units was modified, as compared to those you have just told us about.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The second map, then, shows the HVO front lines and pockets that develops after April '93, and also shows the changes in brigades of the various sides after different actions occurred up until that time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be possible now to present the central map for Central Bosnia -- the second map. Could you tell us the main changes that occurred between the month of April and the period beginning with July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I show that the lines that developed -- the first one is the front line that developed around the Vitez pocket. The pocket also developed in the Kiseljak area, and also another HVO area -- pocket within the Vares area, which lasts to about November '93. In June, '93 a front line developed between the ABiH and the HVO in the Zepce area, which is shown. And also a split develops and a front line came between the HVO and the ABiH in the Gornji Vakuf area, which is shown to the side. The conflict for this started in July, and the information comes from BritBat reports from early August '93, for the Gornji Vakuf area. The main changes we saw within the brigades: In the Zenica area, the Jure Francetic Brigade was driven out of the Zenica area, and the remnants of the brigade moved into the Vitez pocket. In the same way in Travnik, the Travnicka Brigade and the Frankopan Brigade were pushed out of Travnik, and the elements left over, reformed in the north of the Vitez pocket. In Zepce, the ABiH 319th Brigade was destroyed by the HVO in the Zepce area. Moving south of the map. In Bugogno, the HVO Brigade was pushed out and destroyed in Bugogno. And the same occurred in Kakanj with the Kotromanic Brigade. It was destroyed by the ABiH in the Kakanj area, and the remnants moved into the Vares pockets. And those were the principal changes on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This new definition of front lines involved redeployment of units that were destroyed. Could you give us some information about the way in which these units that were defeated on the ground were absorbed into other units.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. Well, on the HVO side, the Frankopan/Travnicka Brigade were reduced in number, but still seemed to operate as a complete unit, but in the northern area of the Vitez pocket. As mentioned, Jure Francetic Brigade, the elements would then seem to have been deployed within HVO units within the whole of Vitez pocket, but in limited numbers. And as mentioned, the remaining elements of the Kotromanic Brigade deployed into the Vares pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is shown on the two maps that you have described that the confrontation lines with the Serbs were frozen; they didn't change during that period, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: When I say "frozen," they were relatively stable, but there was movement along those front lines. And there was also the same in the Vitez pockets and to some extent in the Kiseljak area. The main activity in the -- against -- in the Serb area was in the area to the west of Travnik, where, for example, the Kamenjas feature was lost to the VRS, and then the ABiH had to retake that feature. And then, from a later date into '93, then continued attacks from the ABiH against the VRS in that area. Other changes were, really, a normal backward and forward movement, but no major changes to the line itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to information at your disposal, was there any evolution regarding the participation of HVO forces on the front line against the Serbs, side by side with the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Going back to January '93, from then we appeared to have seen documents which show a reduction in the forces, the HVO forces on the front line in that area. Then BritBat reports show HVO troops in this area mentioned before up until around June '93. At this point, that seems the last time they were seen on that front line, and BritBat reported that the HVO withdrew, the VRS took their positions, and the ABiH had to retake them at a later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have shown us the list of units and their deployment. It is necessary, on the basis of the figures and the headquarters, to give us some indication as to the importance, the size and strength of those units.
