utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I was a little -- maybe this is my fault, but I didn't understand the sources upon which you based your estimates of HVO troop strength. I thought you said that one of the sources was the assessment on the opposing side, the ABiH. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: -- an ABiH assessment, and then we also had HVO assessments which gave a comparative figure, but for a different time period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The only HVO source that I could find was the special assessment that Colonel Blaskic actually filled out sometime in the late summer of 1993, and I believe that's footnote 64 of your materials. I'm sorry to make you go back and forth between your source materials, Mr. Elford, but this is a somewhat significant point.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With me? All right. If you could turn to page 20 of that report. It actually contains an assessment or a survey of troop strength, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, comparing the figures that you've arrived at in your formal report here, you say for the Viteska Brigade a troop strength of 2.700 in July of 1993, but Colonel Blaskic's records say that the troop strength is actually considerably lower than that at 2172; correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier on that the highest reported figure was 2.700, but for August, and also again in the later period, it was a figure somewhere about 2.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The troop strength estimates contained on page 20 of Colonel Blaskic's 1993 troop strength assessment basically give an evaluation of the troop strength of the Viteska Brigade, the Travnicka Brigade, Frankopan, Stjepan Tomasevic, Nikola Subic-Zrinjski, Jure Francetic, Vitezovi, and the 4th Battalion of the military police, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And according to Colonel Blaskic's assessment, the 4th Battalion of the military police contained only 150 soldiers, not 450, as you stated in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The figure of 450 is throughout Central Bosnia and included elements in places such as Zepce, Kiseljak. So I think this figure is purely for the Vitez pocket itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, there's no question that the 4th Battalion of the military police was under the command and control of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone generally, and Colonel Blaskic particularly, is there?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I haven't put a great deal of study into that part of it, but that appears ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military analyst, you would conclude that that is the case, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I think that's one for -- for the -- it's something which came up within other trials which I haven't looked at yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the Vitezovi? There's a figure of 75 mentioned in Colonel Blaskic's report. Do you have any reason to conclude that that figure is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's why I gave the figure up to the high figure of 180, which came out in court testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, totting up the figures in your -- excluding the Edvard Kvaternik Brigade and the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, totting up the figures that you've given in your report for troop strengths, I come up with a number of about 10.513. Let me just put it to you, you can do the mathematics yourself, but the contemporaneous estimate given by Colonel Blaskic is actually 6.820. Does that sound out of line to you?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The figure 10.000 sounds -- that figure sounds within line, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just two matters of detail. You dealt with members of the Ludvig Pavlovic detachment and stated that they came from Herzegovina, apparently, but that conclusion was based only upon General Blaskic's testimony, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: And also in witness testimony to the arrival -- I mean, we're not clear on the time period they stayed for. But from January of 1993, it appears that they were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But you have no information that any members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade or the Bruno Busic Brigade were in Central Bosnia in April of 1993, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Well, the Ludvig Pavlovic and Bruno Busic, there were elements in Novi Travnik, then also in Gornji Vakuf. We're not sure if that's the same elements or not that moved to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to determine who the brigade commanders were in the performance of your duties at all, or was that something that you did not pay attention to?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I've come across them, but I haven't committed them to memory because they were not part of the report that we've given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, looking at pages 7 and 8 of your report, it looks to me as if the HVO suffered fairly serious attrition in seven of the eleven brigades; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Perhaps if I say the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Looking at the figures we were given for April 1993, the assessment we had was for later in 1993, and that was -- you see that the Travnik Brigade has some variation; the Frankopan, there is a large variation, and we know that is the brigade that was forced out of the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just take them one by one, if we can do so, in short order. The Edvard Kvaternik Brigade, it's not the Eugen Kvaternik, it's actually the Edvard Kvaternik Brigade, isn't it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen both spellings, both variations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This brigade, as we know, was basically eliminated in the fighting around Bugojno, in the late summer of 1993; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Pushed from Bugojno, and then the remnants were moved from the Central Bosnia area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "pushed," is that a military euphemism for defeated?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Defeated by the ABiH, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Travnicka Brigade was also pushed or defeated in Travnik, in June of 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes. It moved in reduced strength to the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, the stragglers that were left after the military defeat moved into the area of responsibility of the Viteska Brigade and tried to reform.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I don't know if "stragglers" is the right terminology, because looking at the Blaskic figures for later in the year, we see a figure of 870, so that's a reduction of just over a hundred, whereas for the other brigades, it was a larger reduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Kotromanic Brigade in Kakanj was basically defeated in the middle of June of 1993, simultaneously with the defeats of the Travnicka and Frankopan Brigades; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica was basically eliminated, all but a couple of hundred soldiers, in April of 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct. Reduced to approximately about 400 troops, is the figure given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Bobovac Brigade, sir, in Vares was basically defeated in early November of 1993 and ejected from the town; right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions about the Zepce forces, sir. The front lines in Zepce were actually pretty much around the town of Zepce itself, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Sorry. The front line that has been shown? Yes. Basically, a line to the south of Zepce that cut off the ABiH positions to the north of it, and [indiscernible] Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the towns of Zepce and the town of Zavidovici, just about four or five kilometres to the north-east, I think. Zavidovici was an ABiH enclave, if you like, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Zepce was an HVO enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: There's a Muslim brigade based in the town as well, so I am unclear about the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to after the defeat of the -- the Muslim Brigade in Zepce became a Croat enclave essentially, didn't it, or an HVO enclave.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: That was not part of this report, but from what I've seen, I'm not quite sure we've got an enclosed enclave. But we know that the Muslim brigades to the north of that town were cut off by the Muslim Brigades -- by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, sir, at page 9, paragraph 30, you make the contention that Colonel Blaskic's assessment that we've referred to in footnote 66 of your report, his assessment of artillery strength did not include the weapons holdings of the HVO Mixed Artillery division. But could you take a look at page 24, sir, of his report -- his special assessment. You'll see that in paragraph 6 of that special assessment, he, in fact, does include the mixed artillery division, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The actual ratio of forces, further back, that divides it by area, and those figures actually tie in with the brigade figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us how many, for example, the total number of 203-millimetre shells that were available to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, according to General Blaskic's -- or Colonel Blaskic's special assessment in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: It states that there was one artillery piece with one shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One shell. All right. And the 120-millimetre units, the 120-millimetre mortars, how many shells did the Central Bosnia Operative Zone have in total for that, for that piece? It was none, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: The mortar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: 120-millimetre, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No shells, right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the testimony that you gave regarding ammunition supplies, could I just ask you to take a look at one of the last documents that I'd like to have marked here as an exhibit. That's a milinfosum from the Prince of Wales Own Regiment, number 92, dated July the 30th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D191/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, the paragraph I'd like you to review is number 2, under "Vitez." Just one preliminary question. You were aware that there was an explosives factory located in Vitez itself, that manufactured the explosive components of an artillery shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the factory did not actually manufacture the shell itself, the hard casing, or the detonators, did it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: No, the explosives factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this milinfosum contains the comment that while supplies of explosive are relatively plentiful, the level of general munitions is running down due to the inability of resupplying the area, but necessity is the mother of invention. Fuses can always be brought in on the periodic helicopter flights into the area. Did you consider this document when you came up with your conclusions that, in 1993, artillery ammunition was plentiful, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Is plentiful the word I used? I said there were problems with supply, but equipment supplies were available. That's what I said for the whole thing, concluding the force ratio is -- you need to know the exact figures, and the exact figures aren't available. But what I had also looked at was reports from the Defence Office, which gave -- reports about the production of supplies during that period, and they talk about numbers of rocket launchers completed, numbers of shells completed, also gun powder produced for the Republic of Croatia, which suggests that there was some form of construction going on, some form of resupply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, though, you would agree with me that there were actual figures available for the latter half of 1993, and they came from no less of an authority than Colonel Blaskic himself, in his special assessment that you relied upon in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any information to lead you to conclude that the recitation of shells available per gun, arranged by brigade, are inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: What is not given, though, was any levels of -- any equipment holding. Yes, we take the figures as being accurate, but I don't know what other supplies there were or what form of replenishment there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you have no reason to believe that Colonel Blaskic's figures are inaccurate, but that there may be other figures that should be taken into account. You just don't know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I believe there are other figures to take into account, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sayers, have you got very much more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: About two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, at page 10, you make some observations regarding the fighting that occurred at Krizancevo Selo, just before Christmas 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and you conclude that there were no casualties there. But let me just ask you whether you've read the testimony of Colonel Williams in this case, or Witness Z that described about 60 or 70 HVO dead during the fighting, just before Christmas of that year?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: It's not clear if this report was referring to what's been described as the massacre at Krizancevo Selo. I take it it's referring to a particular attack on a particular day. I'm not sure if that is the same one. And the report said that the attack was stopped, and this was achieved because of the result of artillery support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not saying that the HVO did not suffer 60 to 70 casualties at Krizancevo Selo immediately before Christmas of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I haven't referred to that in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And my final question is, as far as you're aware, there were no HV units or detachments deployed anywhere in the Busovaca/Vitez pocket, Kiseljak pocket, Vares pocket, or Zepce pocket, were there?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: I haven't studied -- I don't know if there were enough to record -- looking at brigade-sized units to start off, I haven't seen reports of anything of that size, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or any battalions of HV forces located in any of those pockets, as far as you're aware, were there?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD
utterances.text: Not that I've seen in preparing this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, Mr. President. That concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, we're going to have to adjourn now because we have some ex parte matters to deal with. How long do you anticipate being with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I guess within one hour or so, I will be done. It's difficult to say, Your Honour, because within that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I guess not more than one hour. I'm sure it will be even a little bit less than that, because my colleague took several of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I detain you for a couple of minutes, just to deal with a couple of administrative matters, bearing in mind that we're not meeting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Mr. Elford is concerned, would you be back, please, on Thursday morning, half past nine, to conclude your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't speak to anybody about your evidence meanwhile, of course, until it's over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps in order to save time, and as Mr. Elford is collecting himself to withdraw, can I run through the administrative matters which don't concern him. Just as a matter of fact, we only lately discovered that we aren't -- that is, the Prosecution only lately discovered that we're not scheduled to sit next Thursday and Friday, and we are making adjustments to deal with that, so far as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pausing there. It was announced some time ago, but if there is difficulty, because we must finish by the 10th of March, the Trial Chamber will be prepared to sit later on various evenings in order to expedite matters, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be an application for a subpoena that's already been signed, the application, and I'll hand that in this afternoon, and I would be grateful if the Chamber could possibly find time to consider it. The Chamber didn't make, I think, a decision about witness -- the sick witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 8, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to deal with various matters in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I indicate, by way of advance notice, that in light of changes for witnesses in Bosnia and Zagreb, I'm going to make an application, which is necessarily provisional, for videolink facilities, and I'm going to suggest Monday, week, Sarajevo; Wednesday, week, Zagreb. That, if it's possible, will enable the relevant people to travel over the weekend to be in Sarajevo on the Monday, travel on the Tuesday, be in Zagreb on the Wednesday. The timetable of evidence and applications for this week is that on Thursday, Mr. Spork -- there's a schedule that's associated with his evidence. Perhaps I can have that distributed for the Chamber in advance. We can also on Thursday and Friday deal with the binders for Kiseljak, Vitez, Novi Travnik, and Ahmici. There's the question of outstanding videos that can conveniently be discussed, there are differing views about that. The tape, it seems to me that the time has come when it simply might save time for me to call the language assistant, who has been in a position to listen to the tape and prepare the amended transcript, and I'll seek to do that, as necessary, on Thursday or Friday. The witness whose statement -- the deceased witness whose statement was admitted by order of the Chamber yesterday was taken by an investigator, who is available here -- she's certainly available on Thursday, I'm not so sure about on Friday -- and I accordingly tender her, so that if there's any question of impropriety being alleged in relation to the taking of that statement, that matter can be dealt with. And if the Defence would be good enough to let me know if they want me to call her, I will make appropriate arrangements, subject to restrictions of time. On Friday, it may well be, if we have time, that I'll call the witness who can deal with the production of exhibits generally. The Chamber will remember that there's a big schedule served with various annotations on it, helpfully placed there now by the Defence, but it may be that to take that witness this week, and for him to deal with the generality of matters, would be helpful, although, of course, the parties -- we are certainly available tomorrow to negotiate with the Defence, if that would help matters, as we're not otherwise sitting. And finally, can I inform the Chamber that the transcripts admitted last week have been collected together; they occupy two binders. The process of annotating them will take some time. I think I was regarded as reckless by my colleagues in making the promise I did, but I stand by my promises, especially when they are responsive to a request from His Honour Judge Bennouna. But I simply say, to have them fully annotated and distributed is undoubtedly going to take until the end of next week, I would have thought, at the earliest. We are entirely in the Chamber's hands, if it would rather have the material unannotated in advance. If so, we'll send them out to copying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's best to stick to the annotations, speaking for myself. Yes. Now, we are anxious to get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been ordered to advise the Court on four witnesses and also some which were put in the category of negotiation with the Prosecution. I am talking about the transcripts. I just wanted to tell you that I am ready to do so. So it is not that we are delaying the issue. We are ready. Whenever you ask, we can provide the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We can do that tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Thursday. Sometime on Thursday we'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are now going to adjourn for quarter of an hour. We shall then sit for what I hope will be a brief ex parte session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
